sections.b: Ezra enters the book as a priest descended from Aaron through Zadok (7:1–5) and as "a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (7:6). The key to his life is 7:10: he gave his heart to searching out the LORD's law, doing it and teaching it. Armed with a letter from Artaxerxes, he leads about 1,500 men and their families from Babylon, refuses an armed escort, and delivers a fortune in gifts to the temple (chapters 7–8). His memoir is written in the first person (7:27–9:15). When officials report marriages with the peoples of the land, he grieves, prays a long confession on behalf of the people (9:6–15), and then presides over a covenant and a court that require the men to send away their foreign wives and children (chapter 10). Readers have admired his humility and devotion to Scripture, and many have been troubled by the outcome of his reform.

common: Ezra is remembered as the priest and scribe who brought the law of Moses back to the center of Jewish life after the exile.
uncommon: Some scholars date Ezra's arrival to 398 BC, after Nehemiah, rather than to 458 BC; a few, following Charles Torrey, have doubted that he existed.

claude.title: Three verbs
claude.body: Claude's reading. Ezra 7:10 sets out a pattern of study, practice and teaching that shapes the rest of his story: he studies the law, keeps it himself (fasting, refusing an escort, guarding the gifts), and only then teaches and enforces it. The order may be the verse's real point, and it is one later Jewish teachers drew out too (Mishnah Avot 1:17).

sections.b: Artaxerxes' letter (7:12–26), in the empire's official Aramaic, shows Persian government at work: the title "king of kings," a council of seven counselors (compare Esther 1:14), the province Beyond the River with its treasurers and satraps (7:21; 8:36), Persian loanwords such as asparna, "exactly," tax exemptions for temple personnel (7:24), and royal penalties backing "your God's law and the king's law" (7:26). The darics of 8:27 were Persian gold coins. Ezra calls the community "slaves" under Persia even while thanking God for the kings' kindness (9:9). Historians compare Ezra's mission with that of the Egyptian official Udjahorresnet, whom Darius I sent home to restore a temple institution, and debate whether Persia formally authorized local laws as royal law.

common: Persian kings generally let subject peoples keep their temples and laws, and Ezra's letter reflects that policy.
uncommon: Some scholars think Persia formally ratified the Torah as imperial law for Judah; others doubt such a policy existed.

sections.b: In his prayer Ezra calls the returned community a peletah, a band of survivors, four times (9:8, 9:13, 9:14, 9:15) and a she'erit, a remnant, once (9:14). God has left them "a tent peg in his holy place" and "a little life again" in their slavery (9:8). The remnant is a gift and a danger: Ezra fears that if they break God's commands again, God might make an end of them "until no remnant and no survivor was left" (9:14). His words draw on Isaiah's hope for the escaped of Judah (Isaiah 10:20–22; Isaiah 37:31–32).

Ezra fasts three times. At the Ahava canal he calls a fast "to humble ourselves before our God" and ask for a safe road, since he had refused a royal escort; God "was moved by our pleading" (8:21–23). When he hears of the marriages he sits in mourning until the evening offering and rises from his ta'anit, his "self-humbling" (9:3–5), the word that later Hebrew uses for a fast and that names the Talmud's tractate on fasts. And after the leaders swear the covenant he goes without food and water in a temple room, as Moses did after the golden calf (10:6; Deuteronomy 9:18).

Ezra's first chapters show outsiders inside the work of the temple. The temple servants, or "given ones," may have been of foreign descent, and the rabbis identified them with the Gibeonites; Ezra recruits 220 more of them (7:7; 8:20; Joshua 9:27). The Persian king funds the temple, calls the LORD "the God of the heavens" and fears his anger (7:12–23).

Officials tell Ezra that the people, priests and Levites have not kept apart from "the peoples of the lands" (9:1). Their list joins the Canaanite nations of Deuteronomy 7:1 with the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians of Deuteronomy 23:3–7, and they call the marriages ma'al, a sacrilege against the "holy seed" (9:2). Ezra's prayer joins laws from Leviticus 18 and Deuteronomy 7 and 23 into one command (9:11–12). Shecaniah proposes a covenant to send out the wives and their children (10:3), and a court of family heads names about 113 men (10:18–44). The Hebrew of the last verse is hard, and only 1 Esdras 9:36 says outright that the wives and children were sent away. Kidner and Williamson read the episode as the protection of a fragile faith community; Christine Hayes as a new idea of holiness by descent; Smith-Christopher and Eskenazi with Judd as the exclusion of Judeans who had never gone into exile; Harold Washington and Willa Johnson as harm done to the weakest; and André LaCocque reads Ruth as a reply to it.

common: Ezra's reform is the Bible's sharpest separation of Israel from its neighbors.
uncommon: Some read Ruth and Isaiah 56 as later protests against Ezra's policy; others date them differently and see no direct response.

sections.h: Marriages ended without divorce papers in Ezra 10
sections.b: The covenant of Ezra 10 ends marriages without the forms of Deuteronomy's divorce law. The verb is "send out" (hotsi'), not the divorce word shillach, and no certificate is mentioned (10:3, 10:19; compare Deuteronomy 24:1). Later rabbinic law explained this by treating such marriages as legally void (Bavli Kiddushin 68b). For the episode as a whole, see the topic on foreigners.

sections.h: Ezra and the law in his hand
sections.b: Ezra is "an expert in Moses' law" (7:6) who set his heart to search it out, do it and teach it (7:10). Artaxerxes sends him to inspect Judah "by the law of your God that is in your hand" and backs it with royal penalties (7:14, 7:25–26). What that law was is debated: the Pentateuch much as we have it, a part such as the Priestly laws or Deuteronomy, or a local law the empire recognized. In chapter 9 Ezra quotes the law by weaving together Leviticus 18 and Deuteronomy 7 and 23, and in chapter 10 Shecaniah applies it to a case it does not directly address (10:3). The scene shows the law becoming a written text to be interpreted, the beginning of the work of the scribes.

sections.b: Ezra himself is a priest of Zadok's line (7:1–5). His caravan includes two priestly houses (8:2), but no Levites until he sends to Casiphia and gets 38 of them and 220 temple servants (8:15–20). Twelve chief priests and twelve Levites guard the gifts as holy men carrying holy things (8:24–30). The royal letter frees all temple staff from tax (7:24). In chapter 10 the list of offenders begins with the high priest Jeshua's own family, and only the priests are said to offer a guilt ram (10:18–19).

Ezra's family tree runs through Zadok to Aaron (7:2), giving him the priestly line Ezekiel said alone could serve at the altar (Ezekiel 44:15). Compared with 1 Chronicles 6:3–15 the list skips six generations, including David's priest Zadok himself, and goes straight from Meraioth to the Azariah who served in Solomon's temple (7:3; 1 Chronicles 6:10). The later Zadok, son of Ahitub, is kept.

sections.h: Shortened lines and lists in Ezra 7–10
sections.b: Ezra's own genealogy (7:1–5) gives sixteen ancestors from Seraiah back to Aaron and leaves out six names that 1 Chronicles 6 includes, showing that a family tree could prove descent without listing every generation. Chapter 8 lists the family heads who traveled with him, most from clans already in Ezra 2, and two clan names lost from the Hebrew (8:5, 8:10) are supplied by the Greek. Chapter 10 closes the book with about 113 men who had married foreign wives, ordered by rank from priests to lay Israel.

In Ezra 8–10 the returned community is still called "the exile" or "the people of the exile" (8:35; 9:4; 10:7–8, 10:16), decades after coming home. Belonging is defined by having gone through exile, while others are "the peoples of the land." Ezra's prayer says they are still slaves, under the kings of Persia, and that the exile's sword, captivity and shame continue "just as we are now" (9:7–9).

Ezra's chapters apply holiness to people, things and descent. The priests and Levites guarding the gifts are "holy men" with "holy things" (8:28). The officials call Israel "the holy seed," a phrase from Isaiah 6:13, and the marriages a sacrilege against it (9:2). The answer is the verb of holiness, badal, "set apart": the people must set themselves apart from the peoples of the land (10:11), echoing Leviticus 20:26, "I have set you apart from the peoples to be mine."

Ezra kneels with open hands at the evening offering and confesses the people's guilt (9:5–15). The prayer belongs with Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9, and like them it builds on Solomon's prayer for repentant exiles (1 Kings 8:46–50). It speaks as "we," though Ezra was not among the guilty, reviews Israel's history, thanks God for a remnant, and ends without a request. Said aloud before a gathering crowd (10:1), it also moved the people to act.

Repentance in Ezra moves from grief to confession to action: Ezra's mourning and prayer (9:3–15), Shecaniah's confession "We are the ones who have acted unfaithfully" and covenant (10:2–3), and Ezra's call to "make your confession to the LORD" and set themselves apart (10:11). The cost of the action, the sending away of wives and children, is what makes this repentance so debated.

Ezra 9:1 names Moabites among the peoples whose daughters must not be married, and 9:12 applies Deuteronomy 23:6, a law about Ammon and Moab. Ruth, a Moabite who joined Israel and became David's great-grandmother, stands in tension with that reading. Some scholars, such as André LaCocque, think the book of Ruth was written or retold as a reply to Ezra's and Nehemiah's policy; others date it earlier. The rabbis held that Deuteronomy 23 barred Moabite men, not women (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3).

Ezra's memoir explains its successes with one refrain: the hand of God was on him (7:6, 7:9, 7:28; 8:18, 8:22, 8:31). The king grants his requests, Levites are found, and the caravan reaches Jerusalem safely, all without miracles. God works through a Persian king's goodwill and the ordinary choices of travelers, as Ezra 1:1 had shown with Cyrus.

sections.b: Ezra 8–10 has several Ketiv-Qere pairs, mostly in names: Zabbud/Zaccur (8:14), Olam/Elam (10:2), Jeremoth/Ramoth (10:29), Kelahai/Keluhu (10:35, where the Leningrad Codex mixes the two), Jaasu/Jaasai (10:37), Jaddo/Jaddai (10:43). In 8:17 the written text has "I sent them out" where the margin reads "I commanded them," and "those who are given" where it reads "the temple servants"; in 10:44 it has "takers of" where the margin reads "they had taken." A few more pairs differ only in spelling. The site's Plain follows the Qere in each case.

sections.b: 1 Esdras 8:1–9:36 retells Ezra 7–10 in a freer Greek, then goes straight on to Ezra's reading of the law (1 Esdras 9:37–55, parallel to Nehemiah 7:73–8:12). It supplies clan names missing from the Hebrew of Ezra 8:5 and 8:10, has 72 lambs (in Codex Alexandrinus; 76 in Codex Vaticanus) for 77 (8:35), Edomites for Amorites (9:1), and "spent the night" for "went" (10:6). It makes the four men of Ezra 10:15 helpers rather than opponents, and it ends the list with "they sent them away with their children" (1 Esdras 9:36), where the Hebrew of Ezra 10:44 is hard. Verse numbers in chapter 8 differ between the KJV Apocrypha and Rahlfs' Greek: Rahlfs runs up to four lower near the end (Rahlfs 8:66 is KJV 8:69; Rahlfs 8:90 is KJV 8:93–94). Chapter 9 is numbered alike.

sections.b: Ezra 7:12–26, the copy of Artaxerxes' letter to Ezra, is the second and last Aramaic section of the book (after 4:8–6:18). It has the marks of an official letter of the Persian chancery: sender and addressee, a greeting ("full greeting"), the transition "and now," and Persian loanwords such as asparna, "exactly," gizzabrayya, "treasurers," and dat, "law." The narrator introduces it in Hebrew (7:11) and returns to Hebrew for Ezra's blessing (7:27).

Ezra's prayer calls the land "a land of defilement," using niddah, the word for menstrual impurity, as a figure for the moral impurity of the peoples' practices (9:11), as Leviticus 18:24–28 speaks of the land made unclean by sin. Scholars debate whether Ezra treats the foreign women as ritually impure or the issue as moral and genealogical.

sections.h: The ban on property in Ezra 10
sections.b: In Ezra 10:8 the verb of the ban, cherem, is used for the property of anyone who refused to come to the assembly: it would be devoted to the temple, and the owner cut off from the community. The old law of war has become a tool of community discipline, the background of later Jewish excommunication (cherem) and of the Talmud's rule on a court's power over property (Bavli Yevamot 89b).

sections.h: Loyal love through a foreign king
sections.b: Twice Ezra says God "stretched out" loyal love (hesed) before the Persian king and his court (7:28; 9:9). Covenant loyalty, usually shown within Israel, here reaches the people through the favor of an empire.
